title: Meeting skills
description: Installs preparing-client-meetings, which turns pull requests and tracker tickets into what to say at dailies and weeklies, in a weekly note in the user's Obsidian vault, and writes a pull request scheduled for a later day into the first meeting after it opens. The vault is found on the local filesystem and the trackers are read through the MCP servers the project already has.

content: description: Prepares what to say at a daily standup or a weekly status meeting from pull requests, merge requests and tracker tickets, across GitHub repositories and GitLab projects on gitlab.com or a self-managed host, plans the coming week's meetings and work, and writes a pull request scheduled with scheduling-pull-requests into the first meeting after it opens, all in a weekly note in the user's Obsidian vault. Every spoken line is short, plain, and traceable to a pull request or ticket. Use when asked to prepare a daily, a standup, a weekly or a status meeting, to say what to report at a meeting, or to plan the week. Not for posting a Linear project update, which writing-linear-updates owns, or for writing anything to a tracker or forge.

compatibility: Needs python3 and the Obsidian vault on the local filesystem; gh with read access for GitHub repositories; for GitLab projects, glab signed in to the host, GITLAB_TOKEN, or a username for public projects read signed out. Reads Jira through the atlassian MCP server and Linear through linear-server when the session has them; without one it reports from the forges alone and says so.

A meeting update answers three questions: what changed since the last meeting, what comes next, and what is in the way. It is spoken, so it is short and plain. **Every line traces to a pull request or a ticket**, or to a pull request scheduled to open before the meeting, and says what will be true when the meeting starts.

A pull request here is a GitHub pull request or a GitLab merge request, and the forge is the service hosting the repository. Both forges are this skill's subject whatever the current project uses: one roster can hold clients on each.

Plain Markdown in the user's Obsidian vault, the directory that contains `.obsidian/`. Find it before writing anything, and if there is none, say so and return the text. **Never write these files into a code repository.**
Meetings.md      the roster: one row per recurring meeting
2026-W40.md      one note per ISO week: the plan, then each meeting

No frontmatter, and a paragraph is one line, because Obsidian shows a single newline as a line break. Read a note before changing it, change only the section you own, and never reword what the user wrote.
`Meetings/Meetings.md` is one line saying what it is, then one table the user fills:
| Acme | daily | Mon–Fri 09:30–09:45 | acme/api, acme/web | Jira ACME |
- **Meeting** is `daily` or `weekly`; a client with both has two rows.
- **When** is local time with an end, so clashes can be seen.

- **Repositories** are `owner/name` on GitHub; `owner/*` means the whole organisation. A GitLab project is `gitlab:group/project`, with any subgroups in the path, and `gitlab:group/*` means the group and its subgroups. On a self-managed or Dedicated host, the host comes first, as in the clone URL: `gitlab:gitlab.example.com/group/project`. A first segment with a dot is read as the host whenever a whole path still follows it, so a top group whose name has a dot is written with its host: `gitlab:gitlab.com/my.group/sub/project`. A value without `gitlab:` is GitHub, so existing rows keep their meaning.
Preparing a meeting works without a row; planning the week needs the rows. Never add a row or a value from a guess; one the user states may be written in.

1. **Identify the meeting.** The request says daily or weekly; a standup is a daily, a status meeting a weekly. With a roster row for it, use the row. Without one, use the repository in the current directory and whichever tracker the session can read, naming the repository from `git remote get-url origin` as the roster would: a github.com remote is `owner/name`, a gitlab.com remote `gitlab:group/project`, and a remote on another host `gitlab:HOST/group/project` when that host is a GitLab, as `glab auth status --hostname HOST` or the project's own instructions show. Ask only when there is neither a row nor a repository, or the remote's host is neither forge.

2. **Find the window**, from the previous occurrence of the meeting to now. With a row, that is the previous slot: Friday's for a daily on Monday. Without one, the same time on the previous working day for a daily, and seven days back for a weekly.

3. **Collect from the forges** with this skill's script, given the repositories as the roster writes them (`owner/*` becomes `--org owner`, `gitlab:group/*` becomes `--org gitlab:group`) and the tracker key when there is one:
python3 <this skill's directory>/scripts/collect.py --repo acme/api --repo acme/web --key ACME --since 2026-09-25T09:30

It prints your pull requests merged or closed without merging in the window, your open ones ready for review with who they wait on, your drafts, the reviews you gave, and pull requests waiting on your review. Lines read `api#39` for GitHub and `billing!39` for GitLab, each forge's own reference; Sources links use the same text. It changes nothing. Exit code 1 names a repository it could not read: say which, and go on.

One call takes GitHub and GitLab values together, as in `--repo acme/api --repo gitlab:gitlab.example.com/acme/billing`. GitHub is read through gh. GitLab is read through glab when it is signed in to that host, and otherwise over HTTPS, with `GITLAB_TOKEN` when it is set for that host. Signed out, GitLab does not know who you are, so the script needs `--gitlab-user` with the user's GitLab username: ask for it once, never guess it from a name. Signed out, gitlab.com also refuses comments, so the output says the reviews you gave are approvals only; say so in the reply.

4. **Read the tracker**, when there is one: your tickets whose status changed in the window, and blockers, meaning a ticket flagged, in a blocked status, or with an open "is blocked by" link. For Jira, through the `atlassian` MCP server: `assignee = currentUser() AND project = ACME AND updated >= "2026-09-25 09:30"`. For Linear, through `linear-server`. Without a row, read the tickets whose keys the pull requests carry. With no tracker, or without its tools in this session, write "Tracker not read" in the note and carry on from the pull requests.
5. **Take Next from this week's plan**: its first items that are not done yet. With no plan, take the drafts and the tracker's in-progress tickets, and say so.

6. **Write the update** into this week's note under `## Mon 28 Sep — Acme daily`, creating the note if needed, and show it in the reply. Without a row, the repository name stands in for the client. Preparing the same meeting again replaces its section.

scheduling-pull-requests hands over a pull request that opens later: the repository, written as the roster writes it, the branch, the opening time, the ticket key, and one plain sentence saying what changed. The work reads as done on the opening day, so it is reported at the first meeting after the opening time, and at no earlier one.
1. **Find the row** for the repository. Without one, write nothing and say so: there is no meeting to report it at.

2. **Find the meeting**: the first occurrence of that row after the opening time. For a Mon–Fri 09:30 daily and an opening on Friday at 17:12, that is Monday's daily. For a Thursday weekly, it is the next Thursday's.

3. **Write its section** in that meeting's ISO-week note, `## Mon 5 Oct — Acme daily` in `2026-W41.md`, creating the note if needed and keeping the meetings in the order they happen. If the section already exists, add the line and leave the rest alone.

4. **Write one line** from the sentence handed over, in plain words. A daily says `**In review:** Invoices can be downloaded as a CSV file.`, and a weekly says `**In progress:** Invoices can be downloaded as a CSV file, in review.`
5. **Write Sources** from what exists, since the pull request has no URL yet: `Sources: csv-export, pull request opening Fri 2 Oct 17:12; ACME-9`.

Write only that line and its Sources. The rest of the meeting is not known yet. Preparing the meeting as usual before it starts replaces the section, and by then the pull request is open and the collector finds it.
- **In review:** what is ready, and who it waits on.
- **Blocked:** what, and who can unblock it; or "nothing".
- **Shipped:** what merged since the last weekly, or was released.
- **In progress:** what is in review or in draft, with its state.
- **Next week:** the top of next week's plan.
- **Decisions needed:** what you need from them, and from whom.

Drop a line with nothing in it, except Blocked, where "nothing" is news. Under the lines, `Sources:` links each pull request and ticket used. It is for checking, not for reading out. Link only URLs you read; a ticket the tracker did not return stays a plain key.

- **Plain words for any audience.** Say what someone who never saw the code would notice. Ticket keys, and schema, model, service or repository names, stay out of spoken lines; they belong in the Sources line and the plan.
- **Say the result, not the method.** "Invoices are no longer sent twice when a payment retries", not "add an idempotency key to the payment webhook".
- **One line per item**, about fifteen words. Several pull requests for one ticket are one item.

- **Rephrase, never add.** Plainer words for what the source says, never an effect it does not state. "Customers can export invoices as CSV" rephrases `feat: export invoices as CSV`; "saves finance a day a month" adds.
- **Merged is not released.** Say released only when a release after the merge exists, such as a merged release pull request or a tag.
- **Closed without merging never counts**, and a claim in its title, such as "twice as fast", goes with it.
- **A draft is in progress, not in review.**
- **No number nobody measured, and no impact no source states.**
- **A blocker names the thing and who can clear it.** "Might be blocked" is a risk; it belongs in Next or nowhere.
- **Nothing new is a valid update.** "Nothing merged since yesterday; the CSV export still waits on review" beats a padded line.

- **Finished work is never presented as still in progress.** Work whose pull request is scheduled to open later is reported from the first meeting after it opens, as "A scheduled pull request" says. To spread work out, schedule its pull request with scheduling-pull-requests instead of saying it is not done.
At the weekend, or when asked to plan the week:

1. **Lay out next week's meetings by day** from the roster, and **name every clash**: two meetings whose times overlap. With an empty roster, say so: the plan covers the current repository's work only, and no clash can be checked.

2. **List the committed work per client**, in the tracker's own order: your tickets in the open sprint or cycle that are not done (Jira: `assignee = currentUser() AND project = ACME AND sprint in openSprints() AND statusCategory != Done ORDER BY Rank`), then your open pull requests on other tickets. Never set a priority or estimate a date. Without a tracker, the open pull requests are the list, and the plan says so.
3. **Write `## Plan`** directly under the first line of next week's note, creating the note if needed. If a plan exists, update it and keep what the user added.
The plan is a list of work, not a script. Each meeting's Next reads from it, and what gets said comes from what actually happened since the last meeting.
The file is named after the ISO week, `2026-W40.md`. No heading at the top: the file name is the title.
| Thu 1 Oct | 09:30 Acme daily, 09:30 Globex weekly |
Clashes: Thu 1 Oct 09:30, Acme daily and Globex weekly.
- ACME-9 Invoice export as CSV (in review, api#39)
- ACME-10 Tax rules in one place (draft, api#41)
Open pull requests only: Globex has no tracker.
- **Done:** Invoices are no longer sent twice when a payment retries.
- **In review:** Invoice export as CSV, waiting on @dana.
Dates are absolute. Meeting sections follow in the order the meetings happen.
- Every spoken line traces to an entry in its Sources line.
- Nothing closed without merging is reported, and no draft is called in review.
- The tracker was read, or the note says it was not.
- No roster value, priority, date, number or impact was guessed.
- Spoken lines are plain; keys and internal names appear only in Sources and the plan.
- The files are in the vault, not in a repository.
- A scheduled pull request appears only under the first meeting after it opens.
